papers.title: Acute Heat Stress Disrupts Hepatic Homeostasis and Gut Microbiota in Early-Juvenile Asian Swamp Eels (Monopterus albus)
papers.abstract: Water temperature is a critical environmental determinant of aquatic organism survival. The Asian swamp eel (Monopterus albus), a major aquaculture species, is highly vulnerable to acute summer heat stress at the early-juvenile stage. Juveniles exposed to 32 °C for 96 h (versus 25 °C controls) exhibited 3498 differentially expressed hepatic genes, with enrichment in amino acid metabolism, immune regulation, and apoptosis pathways; immunity, metabolism, and ion binding were top enriched functions. Key genes linked to immune activation, apoptosis, and metabolic reprogramming were upregulated. Gut 16S rRNA profiling revealed increased microbial diversity and taxonomic shifts indicative of microbiota disruption. These findings show that acute heat stress disrupts hepatic homeostasis via coordinated inflammatory, apoptotic, and metabolic responses while altering gut microbiota, offering an integrated view of thermal resilience mechanisms in early-life-stage teleosts.

papers.title: Silent Infection, Early Warning: Animals as Candidate Sentinels for Crimean–Congo Haemorrhagic Fever Surveillance—A Systematic Review
papers.abstract: Crimean–Congo haemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) is a widely distributed tick-borne arbovirus maintained in an enzootic cycle involving wild and domestic mammals and ixodid ticks, particularly Hyalomma. This systematic review synthesised 390 eligible publication-level reports published from 2015 through 31 August 2026, comprising 351 independent quantitative reports and 39 linked/nonadditive publications. The evidence tables contained 150 animal, 106 tick and 180 human records across 69 countries. Serology dominated animal investigations; among reports with species-specific raw counts, antibody positivity was highest in camels (72.9%; 3918/5377 across 23 reports), followed by red deer (41.4%) and cattle (25.1%). Among 106 tick reports, CCHFV-positive Hyalomma and Rhipicephalus were reported in 80 (75.5%) and 41 (38.7%), respectively. Human sensitivity analyses yielded median estimates of 3.8% for antibody positivity, 13.6% for direct/composite viral detection and 20.0% for case fatality. These summaries are descriptive rather than pooled prevalence estimates. Overall, the evidence supports livestock and tick surveillance as complementary components of One Health surveillance, while prospective temporal studies are needed to establish predictive early-warning performance.

papers.title: Wildlife as a Potential Reservoir of Paratuberculosis: Molecular Evidence of Mycobacterium avium Subspecies paratuberculosis in a Biosphere Reserve, the Sudan
papers.abstract: Mycobacterium avium subspecies paratuberculosis (MAP) causes paratuberculosis (PTB), a chronic wasting enteritis of domestic and wild ruminants. Although the disease and/or its aetiology have been reported in livestock in the Sudan, they have not been investigated in wild animals. This study investigated MAP DNA prevalence in the Dinder National Park (DNP) to provide baseline data on PTB in wildlife. Fresh faecal samples (n = 274) of wild ruminants were collected from the ground around the six major water ponds of the DNP (44–48 samples/pond). Faecal DNA was extracted using a rapid extraction protocol and tested for MAP DNA using a real-time recombinase-aided amplification (RAA) assay. The vegetation structure around the ponds was observed and described. MAP DNA detection rates around the ponds ranged between 64.4% and 22.9%, with an overall apparent prevalence of 37.9% and a sensitivity/specificity-adjusted sample positivity of 42.4%. The faecal samples belonged to Reedbuck (Redunca redunca), Warthog (Phacochoerus aethiopicus), Waterbuck (Kobus defasa), African Buffalo (Syncerus caffer), Oribi (Ourebia ourebia), and among which MAP DNA detection rates were 39.4% (28/71), 39.1% (18/46), 38.0% (27/71), 37.5% (12/32) and 35.2% (19/54), respectively. The vegetation pattern around the ponds showed a notable difference that was consistent with MAP DNA detection. These results are consistent with the potential role of wildlife in paratuberculosis maintenance and transmission. Future investigations, including genotyping, would identify possible cross-transmission of the pathogen at the wildlife-domestic animal interface.

papers.title: The Application of Artificial Intelligence in Brucellosis: Diagnosis, Genomic Analysis, Epidemiological Prediction and Drug Discovery
papers.abstract: Brucellosis, a globally significant zoonosis caused by Brucella, poses a substantial impediment to the sustainable development of the livestock industry and threatens public health security. Traditional control and prevention strategies for brucellosis suffer from fundamental limitations. These include the time-consuming, biosafety risks associated with bacterial culture and the difficulty in differentiating between natural infection and vaccine-induced immunity with serological tests. There remains a challenge in accurately distinguishing vaccine strains from wild-type strains via genotyping methods. Furthermore, current practice relies on manual reporting and empirical judgment without real-time data support. Consequently, these challenges could hinder early detection and reduce the efficiency of large-scale screening, which leads to imprecise outbreak tracing and fails to meet the practical demands of modern livestock production for rapid diagnosis, intelligent prevention and control. In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) technologies have been widely applied in the field of veterinary microbiology, which could offer novel technical pathways for the prevention and control of brucellosis. This paper reviews the latest research progress in the application of AI for the rapid diagnosis of brucellosis, genomic analysis and antimicrobial resistance prediction of Brucella, epidemiological risk early warning and the development of drugs and vaccines. We further analyze the current limitations of AI in brucellosis research including the scarcity of high-quality, annotated datasets, insufficient model interpretability and low efficiency in on-site translation and implementation. The paper provides an outlook on the future development of AI-based intelligent prevention and control systems for brucellosis, which offer a theoretical reference and innovative perspectives for the fundamental research and clinical application of AI technologies. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first review to integrate AI applications across the entire chain of brucellosis prevention and control and to propose a conceptual framework for AI-driven intelligent brucellosis management.

papers.title: Integrative Multi‐Omics Analysis Identifies Candidate MicroRNA Regulatory Networks Associated With High‐Altitude Adaptation in Tibetan Pigs
papers.abstract: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are key posttranscriptional regulators of gene expression and play important roles in physiological responses to hypoxia, particularly in the cardiovascular system. However, the regulatory roles of miRNAs in cardiopulmonary tissues during high‐altitude adaptation remain poorly understood. Tibetan pigs are a high‐altitude‐adapted breed with strong hypoxia tolerance, making them an ideal model for investigating the molecular mechanisms underlying high‐altitude adaptation. In this study, we compared miRNA expression profiles between Tibetan pigs and low‐altitude Meishan pigs and integrated multi‐omics data to investigate miRNA‐mediated regulatory networks, with a particular focus on target genes and 3'UTR genetic variation. Small RNA and mRNA sequencing of heart and lung tissues identified 70 differentially expressed miRNAs and 453 candidate target genes associated with hypoxia adaptation, which were significantly enriched in pathways such as vascular smooth muscle contraction. Integrative analysis of whole‐genome resequencing data from 20 Tibetan pigs and 17 Meishan pigs further revealed that genetic variants within 3'UTR regions may contribute to the modulation of miRNA‐mRNA interactions. Notably, we identified a highly differentiated SNP within the predicted miR‐221‐5p binding site in the 3'UTR of RAB17 , suggesting a potential role of this variant in posttranscriptional regulation. Dual‐luciferase reporter assays and functional validation further supported a regulatory interaction between miR‐221‐5p and the RAB17 3'UTR. Collectively, these findings provide an integrative multi‐omics framework for elucidating candidate miRNA regulatory networks associated with high‐altitude adaptation and highlight the potential contribution of miRNA‐mediated posttranscriptional regulation and 3'UTR genetic variation to high‐altitude adaptation in Tibetan pigs.

papers.title: ABCB1 Frameshift Deletion in Skye Terriers With Potential Pharmacogenetic Relevance
papers.abstract: Ivermectin‐associated neurotoxicity is a potentially life‐threatening condition caused by disruption of the ABCB1 encoded P‐glycoprotein drug transporter in certain dog breeds. Skye terriers are considered at increased risk of ivermectin toxicity despite the absence of an identified molecular cause. We searched the Dog10K variant dataset for ABCB1 variants potentially underlying ivermectin sensitivity in Skye terriers and screened an independent cohort of 27 dogs to confirm sequence variants. A 1‐bp frameshift deletion predicted to cause loss of function in ABCB1 was identified in two of three Skye terriers in the Dog10K dataset and was absent from all 1869 non‐Skye‐terrier genomes. The variant had an allele frequency of 16.7% in the independent Skye terrier cohort. This is the first reported ABCB1 variant in Skye terriers and represents a plausible candidate genetic basis for the anecdotally observed ivermectin sensitivity in the breed.

Molecular modelling study on Piper betle phytocompounds to discover the potential active moiety responsible for xanthine oxidase inhibition in avian gout
papers.abstract: 1. This study investigated the phytochemicals responsible for xanthine oxidase (XO) inhibitory activity in Piper betle L. herb. In silico analysis was performed against the active sites of XO using 32 phytocompounds from P. betle along with the known inhibitor allopurinol used in avian gout treatment.2. Functions including docking score and GLIDE score, ADME analyses using QikProp module and toxicity assessment with ProTox-II server. Molecular dynamics simulations were performed for 100 ns with GROMACS software to evaluate the stability and fluctuations of the protein–ligand complexes.3. The results revealed that 12 phytocompounds of P. betle exhibited higher GLIDE XP docking scores (−6.881 to −4.766 kcal/mol) compared to allopurinol (−4.535 kcal/mol) and 11 phytocompounds showed higher GLIDE energy (−42.822 kcal/mol to −36.706 kcal/mol) than allopurinol (−32.676 kcal/mol). Among these, 4-chromanol and 4-allyl-1,2-diacetoxybenzene were identified as the most potent compounds of P. betle, forming hydrogen bond interactions with XO similar to allopurinol.4. The ADME analyses showed that selected phytocompounds met the ADME descriptors and did not violate Lipinski’s ‘rule of five’ and toxicity assessment yielded satisfactory results. Furthermore, 100 ns MD simulations showed a stable trajectory and less conformational variation (RMSD, RMSF) along with a steady interaction profile observed throughout the simulations. The MM‑GBSA calculations supported the docking studies.5. The data showed that 4-chromanol and 4-allyl-1, 2-diacetoxybenzene phytocompounds present in P. betle might account for antigout activity through XO inhibition, meaning that these could be developed as potential drug molecules.

papers.title: Sanitisation of Enterococcus cecorum attached to the shells of fertilised eggs by carbon dioxide microbubbles and sodium hypochlorite
papers.abstract: 1. Enterococcus cecorum (EC) infection in chicks must be prevented because of its severe pathogenicity in poultry farming. In this study, the combined sanitising effects of sodium hypochlorite (NaClO) and carbon dioxide microbubbles (CO2MB) on artificially applied EC on eggshells were clarified and the effectiveness for sanitising fertilised eggs was investigated.2. The number of surviving EC cells on eggshells decreased with increasing chlorine concentration and treatment time, with the NaClO solution containing CO2MB. The spray treatment of the NaClO solution containing CO2MB was more effective for sanitising EC.3. In addition, sanitisation of EC on fertilised eggs using a NaClO solution containing CO2MB was effective in preventing contamination in the setter, without negative effects on hatching or early growth of chicks.4. Using NaClO solution containing CO2MB was an effective method for sanitising EC on fertilised eggs.

papers.title: Magnolol enhances yak oocyte maturation and blastocyst quality by improving lipid metabolism and redox homeostasis through a PPARγ-dependent mechanism
papers.abstract: Background Reproductive efficiency in yaks is limited by the poor developmental competence of their oocytes during in vitro maturation (IVM). Magnolol (MAG), a natural polyphenolic compound with potent antioxidant activity, has been reported to regulate cellular metabolism and oxidative stress; however, its role in oocyte maturation and early embryonic development remains unclear. Therefore, this study investigated the effects and molecular mechanisms of MAG on yak oocyte maturation and developmental competence. Methods Yak cumulus–oocyte complexes were cultured in IVM medium supplemented with different concentrations of MAG (0, 0.5, 1, 5, and 10 μmol/L). Oocyte maturation, cumulus expansion, oxidative stress indicators, mitochondrial function, apoptosis, and lipid metabolism were evaluated using fluorescence staining, qPCR, and immunofluorescence analysis. Network pharmacology and molecular docking were used to predict potential targets of MAG, and the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARγ) antagonist GW9662 was applied to verify the regulatory mechanism occurring during IVM and subsequent embryo development. Results Based on the concentration-screening results, 1 μmol/L MAG was selected for subsequent mechanistic and embryo-development analyses. MAG supplementation significantly improved oocyte maturation and cumulus expansion, enhanced glutathione levels and mitochondrial membrane potential, and reduced reactive oxygen species accumulation and apoptosis. MAG also promoted lipid droplet accumulation and upregulated the expression of lipid metabolism–related genes, including PPARG , CD36 , FABP3 , and FABP4 . Network pharmacology identified PPARγ as a key target of MAG. Pharmacological inhibition of PPARγ with GW9662 markedly reversed MAG-induced improvements in lipid metabolism, antioxidant capacity, and oocyte developmental competence. Furthermore, MAG increased blastocyst formation rate, total cell number, and CDX2 expression while reducing the blastocyst apoptosis. Conclusion MAG improves yak oocyte quality and embryonic developmental competence by promoting lipid homeostasis, maintaining redox balance, and enhancing mitochondrial function. The beneficial effects of MAG are closely associated with the involvement of PPARγ signaling in the regulation of lipid homeostasis. These findings provide a potential strategy for improving the efficiency of yak assisted reproductive technologies.

papers.title: The Chromosomal Organization of Isleria hauxwelli and Its Meaning for the Karyotypic Evolution in Thamnophilidae (Passeriformes)
papers.abstract: The order Passeriformes, the most speciose avian order, includes over 6000 species (~60% of all birds). The Amazon Basin alone hosts > 900 bird species, with Passeriformes representing > 500 of them. The family Thamnophilidae comprises ~200 insectivorous species, accounting for 15% of Neotropical passerine richness. Within Thamnophilinae, Isleria is the least speciose genus, containing only two species. It was erected after phylogenetic analyses revealed Myrmotherula as non‐monophyletic. To advance knowledge of chromosomal evolution in Passeriformes, we analyzed the karyotype of Isleria hauxwelli using molecular cytogenetics. We found a diploid number of 2n = 84 and a fundamental number (FN) of 92. The BOE‐7 probe, corresponding to the ancestral fusion of GGA‐9 with two microchromosomes, maintained that configuration without undergoing fission to produce IHA‐5. The BOE‐14 probe, typically fragmented in all cytogenomically characterized Passeriformes, corresponded to two distinct GGA segments: the R3 portion and a region of unknown homology. This is the first documentation of such chromosomal organization in passerines. The absence of these fissions suggests a possible autapomorphic chromosomal condition within Thamnophilidae. Additionally, a potential fission involving microchromosomes homeologous to probes BOE‐15 and BOE‐16 is suggested: while these probes mark three microchromosome pairs in GGA, they mark four pairs in I. hauxwelli —a feature not yet observed in other passerines. As most Thamnophilidae remain cytogenetically uncharacterized, systematic study of this family is essential to determine whether these rearrangements represent synapomorphies, autapomorphies, or convergent events.

papers.title: ZBED6 deletion activates FNDC1-mediated PI3K/AKT and MAPK/ERK1/2 signaling pathways to promote myogenesis in pigs
papers.abstract: Background Myogenesis is a tightly regulated biological process that is essential for skeletal muscle growth, regeneration, and livestock production. Although the transcription factor ZBED6 is a key regulator of skeletal muscle development, the downstream molecular mechanisms through which it controls myogenesis remain incompletely understood. Here, using ZBED6-deficient pigs and primary porcine skeletal muscle satellite cells, we sought to identify novel downstream targets of ZBED6 and elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying ZBED6-mediated regulation of myogenesis. Results By integrating transcriptomic, quantitative proteomic, and ChIP-seq datasets, we identified fibronectin type III domain-containing protein 1 (FNDC1), a muscle-derived secreted factor, as a previously unrecognized direct transcriptional target of ZBED6. ChIP-qPCR and dual-luciferase reporter assays showed that ZBED6 directly binds to the FNDC1 promoter and represses its transcription. Functional analyses in primary porcine skeletal muscle satellite cells showed that ZBED6 knockdown markedly promoted myoblast proliferation, differentiation, and myotube formation, whereas FNDC1 knockdown partially attenuated these effects. Conversely, FNDC1 overexpression partially rescued the impaired myogenesis caused by ZBED6 overexpression. Mechanistically, ZBED6 deficiency promoted porcine myoblast proliferation and differentiation, at least in part, through FNDC1 -mediated activation of the PI3K/AKT and MAPK/ERK1/2 signaling pathways. Consistently, pharmacological inhibition of either pathway significantly attenuated the enhanced porcine myoblast proliferation and differentiation induced by ZBED6 deficiency, supporting that activation of these signaling pathways contributes in part to the pro-myogenic effects mediated by the ZBED6-FNDC1 regulatory axis in porcine myoblasts. Conclusions This study identifies FNDC1 as a novel direct transcriptional target of ZBED6, supporting the ZBED6-FNDC1 axis as a regulatory mechanism contributing to porcine myoblast proliferation and differentiation. These findings expand the current understanding of the ZBED6 regulatory network and provide a cellular framework for future studies investigating skeletal muscle growth in vivo.

papers.title: Chestnut–quebracho tannins shape the fecal metabolome of weaned pigs through microbiota-dependent urolithin production
papers.abstract: Background Chestnut and quebracho tannins may support gut health in weaned piglets, but their efficacy likely depends on farm environment and microbial capacity to convert tannins into bioactive metabolites. This study evaluated the effects of a blend of chestnut-derived hydrolysable tannins and quebracho-derived condensed tannins on growth performance, diarrhea occurrence, gut metagenome, and fecal metabolome in piglets reared under two commercial farm conditions. A total of 160 weaned piglets (initial body weight 6.53 ± 0.13 kg) were assigned to a 2 × 2 factorial design comprising 2 weaning units (W1 and W2) and 2 dietary treatments (control diet or control diet + 2 g/kg tannin blend; 40 piglets per treatment × farm). The trial lasted 76 d, with weighings at T0 (entry into weaning, median 28 d), T1 (d 35), T2 (d 49), and T3 (d 76). Fecal scores and samples were collected at T1, T2, and T3 for shotgun metagenomics (155 samples per time point) and untargeted metabolomics, and targeted urolithin quantification was performed in tannin-treated piglets at T1 and T2. Results Tannin supplementation did not affect overall growth performance throughout the weaning phase, but reduced diarrhea occurrence at T2 in W2 ( P = 0.032). Species-level beta diversity was consistently affected by treatment across time points ( R 2 = 0.01–0.03; P < 0.01), whereas alpha diversity was mainly farm-driven during the early post-weaning phase. Linear discriminant analysis effect size identified farm-dependent taxonomic markers, including Escherichia coli in control pigs from W1 at T1 and Megasphaera elsdenii , Faecalibacterium prausnitzii , and Lactobacillus amylovorus in tannin-treated pigs at later time points. Untargeted metabolomics revealed treatment-related fecal signatures, with isourolithin A and urolithin B among the most discriminant metabolites in treated pigs, especially in W2. Targeted analysis identified 3 urolithin metabotypes (metabotype B in 50.0% of samples), with higher isourolithin A, urolithin B, and urolithin A in W2 than W1 at T2 ( P < 0.01). Network integration identified candidate cooperative microbial consortia associated with urolithin production, including Ellagibacter isourolithinifaciens ; these co-abundance associations are correlative and remain to be functionally validated. Conclusions Overall, chestnut–quebracho tannins were associated with a farm-dependent reduction in post-weaning diarrhea and modulated the gut ecosystem through microbiota-dependent polyphenol metabolism.

papers.title: The mLOS Open-Source Software for Analyzing Length of Stay in Animal Shelters
papers.abstract: Length of stay (LOS) is critical in shelter management and animal welfare. Its assessment by calendar period must account for animals whose stay overlaps with period boundaries. mLOS is an open-source R tool that uses animal-level intake and outcome records to analyze LOS distributions and competing outcomes using survival-analysis methods. A companion Python package, ShelterDataPrep, prepares raw data extracts for analysis. The factors used are calendar period, intake type, and a user-defined animal group. The counting-process formulations left-truncate stays in progress at the beginning of a period and right-censor stays ongoing at period end. Kaplan-Meier estimates the stay distribution, Aalen-Johansen gives cumulative incidence by outcome type, and Cox and Weibull regressions compute the effect of each factor adjusted for others. A run computes in-care stay curves, remaining stay curves, competing outcomes, outcome conditional on tenure, and population-load figures including census. Each is produced for the unified sample and separately by factor. Pooled and per-factor Cox regressions produce hazard ratios while corresponding Weibull regressions produce LOS ratios. Validation includes hand-derived exact tests and simulation fixtures that recover known behavior. The outputs comprise plots, companion CSVs, a JSON with complete results, a consolidated workbook, and an experimental slide deck.

papers.title: Apparent Ca Test Positivity and Crossmatch Reactivity in Donkeys from Italy: Intraspecies and Horse–Donkey Compatibility
papers.abstract: Blood group distribution and serological compatibility are poorly characterized in donkeys. We estimated the apparent Ca positive-test frequency in 84 domestic donkeys and assessed donkey–donkey and horse–donkey crossmatch reactivity. Ca typing was performed using a commercial equine immunochromatographic assay. For donkey–donkey crossmatching, one major and one minor crossmatch were analyzed for each of the 77 Ca-concordant and 34 Ca-discordant pairs. Fifty-six of eighty-four donkeys yielded a positive result with the equine Ca assay (66.7%; 95% CI, 56.1–75.8%). Major combined macroscopic/microscopic reactivity occurred in 18/77 Ca-concordant and 11/34 Ca-discordant pairs, whereas minor combined reactivity occurred in 21/77 and 8/34 pairs, respectively. In crossed random-effects logistic models, the adjusted odds ratios for Ca-discordant versus Ca-concordant pairs were 1.56 (95% CI, 0.64–3.82) for major combined reactivity, 0.82 (95% CI, 0.32–2.10) for minor combined reactivity, and 1.57 (95% CI, 0.41–5.94) for major macroscopic reactivity; the minor macroscopic model was not estimable. Horse–donkey reactions were frequent and direction-dependent. When donkey plasma was tested against horse RBCs, combined reactivity occurred in 80/80 tests in the horse-donor/donkey-recipient dataset and in 76/76 tests in the reciprocal dataset, with macroscopic reactivity in 77/80 (96.3%) and 74/76 (97.4%), respectively. In the reciprocal horse-plasma/donkey-RBC direction, combined reactivity occurred in 53/80 (66.3%) and 51/76 (67.1%) tests, with macroscopic reactivity in 32/80 (40.0%) and 32/76 (42.1%), respectively. Ca concordance was not significantly associated with crossmatch reactivity in the present dataset, and Ca status alone did not account for the observed crossmatch-reactivity pattern.

papers.title: Superior MAP–EtCO2 Target Attainment with Rocuronium-Facilitated Controlled Ventilation in Geriatric Small Dogs: A Retrospective Cohort Study
papers.abstract: Comparative evidence for integrated ventilation–neuromuscular blockade–reversal strategies is limited in geriatric small dogs. This single-center retrospective cohort included 288 dogs aged ≥12 years and weighing ≤7 kg undergoing orthopedic surgery or thoracolumbar hemilaminectomy. Initially planned strategies were spontaneous ventilation without neuromuscular blockade (A), controlled ventilation without blockade (B), rocuronium–controlled ventilation–sugammadex (C), vecuronium–controlled ventilation–sugammadex (D), or vecuronium–controlled ventilation–neostigmine–atropine (E). The primary outcome was the percentage of the entire primary physiologic window with concurrent mean arterial pressure ≥ 60 mmHg and end-tidal carbon dioxide 35–55 mmHg. Adjusted means were A 58.9%, B 59.3%, C 86.6%, D 74.0%, and E 67.8%. Group C exceeded A, B, and D by 27.7 (95% confidence interval, 26.3–29.2), 27.3 (25.9–28.8), and 12.7 (11.2–14.1) percentage points; B and A differed by 0.4 points (−0.8–1.6). Ventilator asynchrony occurred in 3.4% of C versus 73.2% of B. Adjusted mean times to normalized train-of-four ratio ≥ 0.90 were 1.41, 2.31, and 7.43 min in Groups C–E, respectively. Observed early respiratory and hard 48 h event risks were 3.4% and 1.7% in C, 40.7% and 18.6% in A, and 44.6% and 17.9% in B. The rocuronium-facilitated strategy was associated with superior concurrent target attainment; nonrandomized strategy selection precludes causal safety conclusions.

papers.title: Integrated Transcriptomic and Metabolomic Analyses Reveal the Whitening of Perirenal Brown Adipose Tissue in Yak Calves
papers.abstract: Brown adipose tissue (BAT) is essential for neonatal thermogenesis; however, in yak, the adipose tissue exhibits age-related changes from a brown-like to a white-like phenotype between postnatal day 1 (P1) and day 30 (P30). This exploratory study aimed to characterize the molecular and metabolic changes underlying this postnatal transition, with a particular focus on thermogenesis and lipid metabolism. Perirenal adipose tissue from yak calves at P1 and P30 was analyzed using phenotypic, transcriptomic (n = 3 per group), and metabolomic (n = 6 per group) approaches. Our results showed that multilocular adipocytes were abundant at P1, whereas unilocular adipocytes were predominant by P30, accompanied by significantly increased triglyceride content (p < 0.05). Transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses identified a total of 1000 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) and 17 differential metabolites between the two stages. From the DEGs, 13 thermogenesis-related genes and 24 lipid metabolism-related genes were selected based on functional relevance, and all 17 differential metabolites were analyzed. Integrative analysis of the transcriptomic and metabolomic datasets further identified 14 key genes related to thermogenesis and lipid metabolism and 6 differential metabolites potentially associated with these metabolic pathways. Among them, CDS2, GPAM, AGPAT2, CPT1C, GADD45B, PLIN1, and metabolites phosphatidylethanolamine (PE), phosphatidic acid (PA), and oxidized phosphatidylserine (PS) may serve as a potential link between lipid deposition and thermogenic metabolism. Fatty acid profiling showed that n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (n-3 PUFAs), such as eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA, 20:5 n-3) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA, 22:6 n-3) were enriched in BAT, while stearic acid (SA, 18:0) and oleic acid (OA, 18:1 n-9) were enriched in WAT. These findings suggest age-related changes in the molecular and metabolic characteristics of postnatal BAT from a thermogenic phenotype toward a lipid-storage state, consistent with a functional transition during adipose tissue development. This provides a molecular framework for understanding BAT phenotypic changes in neonatal yaks and identifies candidate targets for future studies investigating the regulation of thermogenesis and lipid metabolism in plateau ruminants.

papers.title: Detection and Phylogenetic Characterization of Canine Distemper Virus (Morbillivirus canis) in Wild Foxes and Badgers from Northern Italy in 2021–2026
papers.abstract: Canine distemper virus (CDV) is a highly contagious multisystemic pathogen posing severe threats to wild carnivores and domestic animals. To investigate CDV circulation and lineage diversity in Piacenza Province, Northern Italy, wildlife surveillance was conducted under the Regional Wildlife Monitoring Plan between 2021 and June 2026. Forty-three wild carnivores—comprising red foxes (Vulpes vulpes), European badgers (Meles meles), wolves (Canis lupus), stone martens (Martes foina), and one jackal (Canis aureus)—were evaluated by necropsy, histopathology and molecular assays (RT-qPCR/RT-PCR). Overall, 12 animals (27.9%, 95% CI: 15.3–43.7; six foxes and six badgers) were confirmed to be CDV-positive. No positivity was found before 2024. Positive animals displayed characteristic lesions, including hemorrhagic enteritis, pulmonary hepatization, and footpad hyperkeratosis. Sequencing of the hemagglutinin (H) gene of the four complete H genes obtained revealed that they belonged to clade A of the European/South American 1 lineage, showing the highest nucleotide identity with Alpine CDV strains from Switzerland and Northern Italy. These results confirm the recent circulation of CDV amongst foxes and badgers in Piacenza. Continuous molecular monitoring and integrated cross-border surveillance remain essential for the effective management of transmission at the interface between wildlife and domestic animals.

papers.title: Comparison of Selected Therapies Within the Step-Up Therapeutic Approach in Canine Chronic Inflammatory Enteropathy
papers.abstract: Canine chronic inflammatory enteropathy (CIE) frequently requires a sequential therapeutic approach in which treatment is escalated according to clinical response. This prospective, open-label clinical study evaluates selected dietary, antimicrobial, microbiome-directed, and corticosteroid interventions used within a step-up treatment strategy in dogs with CIE under routine clinical conditions. Fifty-six dogs were enrolled. Clinical response was assessed using the Canine Chronic Enteropathy Clinical Activity Index (CCECAI), together with faecal calprotectin, serum folate, and serum cobalamin concentrations. In the dietary stage, both novel-protein and hydrolysed diets significantly reduced CCECAI and faecal calprotectin. Clinical remission, defined as a final CCECAI score ≤ 3, was achieved in 64% and 60% of dogs, respectively. Baseline-adjusted analyses likewise showed no significant between-group differences in CCECAI, faecal calprotectin, or cobalamin. In dogs receiving second-line treatment, both metronidazole and probiotics combined with fibre significantly reduced CCECAI and faecal calprotectin, while baseline-adjusted comparisons demonstrated no significant differences between treatments for the evaluated outcome. In dogs receiving corticosteroid-containing treatment, substantial numerical reductions in CCECAI and faecal calprotectin were observed in both the prednisone-containing and budesonide-containing regimens; however, the very small subgroup sizes and concomitant dietary, probiotic, and fibre interventions precluded definitive conclusions regarding the specific effects or comparative efficacy of the individual corticosteroids. These findings provide real-world clinical evidence supporting a structured step-up approach to canine CIE and provide a rationale for larger, adequately powered controlled studies to determine whether non-antibiotic microbiome-directed strategies and locally acting corticosteroid-containing therapy can reduce reliance on empirical antimicrobial treatment and systemic corticosteroids, thereby minimising the potential adverse consequences associated with these therapies.

papers.title: Locomotor-State Dependence of Neuromodulation During Avian Free Flight
papers.abstract: Complex avian locomotor behaviors depend on the coordinated operation of neural processes involved in sensory perception, decision-making, and motor execution. Exogenous neural stimulation can alter motor output by intervening in neural processes, but its effects may depend on the current locomotor state. Here, we investigated the locomotor-state dependence of formatio reticularis medialis mesencephali (FRM) microstimulation in freely flying pigeons. Individualized stimulation parameters were screened under stable laboratory conditions and kept constant during free-flight experiments. Flight-state features before and during stimulation were extracted, and state–response models were constructed to quantify their associations with stimulation-evoked turning responses. Results showed that flight state during stimulation was more closely associated with turning responses than pre-stimulation state, with acceleration during stimulation making the largest contribution. When acceleration during stimulation was above the individual mean, turning-response dispersion decreased by 32.92%. In addition, pre-stimulation angular velocity was positively associated with acceleration during stimulation, indicating that the pre-stimulation locomotor state contains information related to the consistency of subsequent stimulation-evoked responses. These findings demonstrate that the effects of FRM microstimulation are locomotor-state dependent and provide a basis for identifying appropriate neuromodulation timing and improving response stability under complex locomotor conditions.

papers.title: Peat Pellets as Enrichment Material for Weaned Piglets
papers.abstract: We aimed to explore the effect of 8 mm peat pellets as enrichment material for weaned piglets. A total of 288 piglets were allocated to one of two treatments: peat pellets (PPs) or chopped straw (CS) as edible enrichment. Twelve pigs were housed per pen, with 12 weaner pens per treatment. Pigs were weighed at day 0, 9, 14, and 28 post-weaning. Faecal consistency was recorded 3 times a week. Piglet behaviour was observed at days 8 and 18, and damage on ears and tail were scored weekly. More cups of edible enrichment were provided to PP pens than to CS pens between day 0–14 to ensure ad libitum availability (p = 0.04). On day 18, PP piglets showed greater exploratory interaction with the edible enrichment than CS piglets (p = 0.045). PPs improved performance in the early post-weaning period, resulting in a higher initial feed intake (p = 0.0498) and growth (p = 0.007) of newly weaned piglets between days 0 and 9, and improved faecal scores between days 14 and 28 (p = 0.007). At the end of the study, piglets had improved body weight uniformity (p = 0.04) and tended to have a lower prevalence of tail damage (p = 0.07) when provided with PPs versus CS. In addition, PP piglets tended to spend less time on ear biting (p = 0.06) on day 8 than CS piglets. PPs are proposed as suitable enrichment material and were associated with improved zootechnical performance and faecal consistency in weaned piglets.

papers.title: Cryopreservation of Cavia porcellus L. Spermatozoa: Microscopic Characterization and Viability
papers.abstract: Studies evaluating the effects of cryopreservation on epididymal spermatozoa of Cavia porcellus remain limited. This study compared the effects of rapid and slow freezing protocols on microscopic characteristics, morphometry, and morphometric correlations. Epididymal spermatozoa from twelve guinea pigs were diluted in OptiXcell® extender with 25% egg yolk and equilibrated at 4 °C for 6 h. One aliquot was evaluated, while the other was cryopreserved using rapid (n = 5) or slow (n = 7) protocols. After thawing, motility, viability, plasma membrane functionality, acrosomal and chromatin integrity, and morphometry were assessed; cooling profiles were characterized using linear and cubic regression models. Cryopreservation reduced microscopic parameters compared with refrigerated samples (p < 0.05). Comparison showed no significant differences in motility, viability, acrosomal integrity, or plasma membrane function (p > 0.05), whereas chromatin integrity was higher after slow freezing (p = 0.03). Rapid freezing reduced acrosomal area, acrosomal perimeter, and head length, whereas slow freezing preserved morphometric variables and correlations, although correlation patterns should be interpreted as associations among morphometric traits rather than structural preservation. Both cooling curves were well described by linear and cubic models. Slow freezing was associated with better preservation of chromatin integrity and selected morphometric characteristics.

papers.title: Primary Erythrophagocytic Low-Grade Splenic T-Cell Lymphoma in a Cat: Clinical Case and Literature Review
papers.abstract: Lymphoma is a common hematopoietic neoplasm in cats; yet hepatosplenic forms remain rare. This report describes a unique case of low-grade erythrophagocytic splenic T-cell lymphoma with suspected peripheral blood involvement in a six-year-old neutered male domestic shorthair cat. The patient presented with severe non-regenerative macrocytic normochromic anemia and moderate splenomegaly. Blood smears revealed mononucleated cells exhibiting erythrophagocytosis. Splenic cytology and flow cytometry were consistent with a reactive process, leading to a presumptive diagnosis of immune-mediated anemia. The condition proved refractory to immunosuppressive therapy with prednisolone and cyclosporine. After splenectomy, histopathology showed diffuse erythrophagocytosis and white pulp hyperplasia. Definitive diagnosis was achieved only by PARR analysis, which demonstrated a monoclonal T-cell receptor gene rearrangement within a polyclonal background. This confirmed a neoplastic T-cell population despite the mature morphology of the lymphocytes. Treatment with chlorambucil and prednisolone resulted in progressive resolution of the anemia. The cat remains alive 13 months after splenectomy. This case highlights the diagnostic challenges of low-grade lymphomas, in which reactive features can mask neoplasia, and underscores the critical role of PARR analysis in differentiating monoclonal T-cell proliferation from complex reactive processes in feline splenic disorders.

papers.title: Single-Nucleus Transcriptomics Identifies Stage-Associated Differences in the Olfactory Epithelium During Natural Sex Reversal in Monopterus albus
papers.abstract: The rice field eel (Monopterus albus) undergoes natural protogynous sex reversal, but whether peripheral sensory tissues differ across sexual stages remains poorly understood. We used single-nucleus RNA sequencing to characterize the olfactory epithelium (OE) of female, intersex, and male rice field eels. After quality control, 22,959 nuclei were retained and classified into 19 cell populations, including olfactory sensory neurons (OSNs), basal/progenitor, epithelial, mesenchymal, endothelial, and immune populations. OE tissues from five individuals within each sexual stage were pooled prior to nuclei isolation, resulting in one pooled snRNA-Seq library per stage; therefore, between-stage comparisons are interpreted as exploratory and descriptive rather than as independently replicated population-level differences. The relative representation of captured nuclei differed among stages, particularly within the sensory neuronal and basal-cell compartments. Pseudotime analysis placed immature OSNs at relatively early transcriptional states associated with ciliated and microvillous OSN populations, whereas CrOSNs were not continuously connected to the principal iOSN–cOSN/mOSN trajectory. Cell-type-specific analyses identified stage-associated transcriptional differences in basal cells and multiple OSN populations. Predicted cell–cell communication profiles also differed among stages, with male OE showing a larger nominal number of inferred interactions but lower overall predicted interaction strength. Expression patterns of ompa, gng8, and ora4 supported the marker-based annotation of major OSN populations within the dataset. These findings provide an exploratory single-nucleus framework for investigating stage-associated variation in the peripheral olfactory system of M. albus.

papers.title: Comparative Bioaccumulation of Mineral Elements in Soft Tissues, Shells, and Pearls of Sinohyriopsis cumingii (Lea, 1852) Cultured for Non-Nucleated, Visceral Mass-Nucleated, and Mantle-Nucleated Pearls
papers.abstract: The triangle sail mussel Sinohyriopsis cumingii (Lea, 1852) is the world’s leading producer of freshwater pearls. Mineral elements are key components of pearls and affect pearl quality, but their bioaccumulation patterns in the soft tissues, shells, and pearls of this species remain unclear. Inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry was used to compare the bioaccumulation of essential major elements (Na, Mg, K, Ca), essential trace elements (Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, Zn, Se, Mo), and non-essential elements (Al, As, Sr, Ag, Cd, Ba, Tl, Pb) in the soft tissues, shells, and pearls of S. cumingii cultured for non-nucleated, visceral mass-nucleated, and mantle-nucleated pearls. Mg, K, Mn, Zn, and Ba were significantly more concentrated in soft tissues than in shells or pearls, whereas Ca and Sr showed the opposite trend (p < 0.05). Principal component analysis based on Zn, Ca, Mg, Sr, and Mn separated soft tissues from shells and pearls, while a second component based on Mo, Fe, Co, and Ni distinguished non-nucleated from visceral mass-nucleated and mantle-nucleated pearl mussels. Ca–Sr and Sr–Ba were consistently positively correlated in soft tissues across all three culture types (p < 0.05). Notably, Na was frequently involved in negative correlations between tissues: in mussels cultured for non-nucleated pearls, shell Na was negatively correlated with soft tissue K and pearl Na with soft tissue Ba (p < 0.05); in those cultured for visceral mass-nucleated pearls, soft tissue Na was negatively correlated with pearl Mn and Zn (p < 0.05); and in those cultured for mantle-nucleated pearls, pearl Na was negatively correlated with shell Zn (p < 0.05). Collectively, these findings elucidate mineral element bioaccumulation in pearl-producing S. cumingii.

papers.title: Quantification of Fecal Glucocorticoid Metabolites in Shelter Cats Using LC/MS/MS: Potential Biomarkers of Stress Associated with Shelter Admission
papers.abstract: Cats can experience physiological stress during transitions to unfamiliar environments, such as shelter admission. To enable non-invasive stress assessment in cats, fecal glucocorticoid metabolites were quantified by liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC/MS/MS) with Girard’s reagent T derivatization. Five analytes were targeted: three glucocorticoids (cortisol, cortisone, and corticosterone) and their fecal metabolites, 11β-hydroxyetiocholanolone and 11-oxoetiocholanolone. Thirty-five cats housed at an animal welfare center were classified into a shorter-admission group (<2 weeks after admission, n = 16) or a longer-admission group (≥2 weeks, n = 19). The three parent glucocorticoids showed no detectable peak in any sample, whereas both metabolites were detected in 28 of the 35 samples and were strongly correlated in both the shorter- and longer-admission groups (ρ = 0.9316 and 0.9699, respectively). Both metabolites were significantly higher in the shorter-admission group (p = 0.0036 and 0.0029, respectively), whereas no significant differences were detected by sex or neuter status. In an incubation experiment, concentration changes within 48 h (≤0.12 ng/mg) were smaller than the between-group differences (1.70–2.16 ng/mg). These findings suggest that both metabolites are potential biomarkers of stress associated with shelter admission and that their measurement may provide a practical, non-invasive approach for monitoring stress in shelter cats.

papers.title: A Marine Bivalve (Entodesma navicula) Extract Suppresses the Replication of Influenza Viruses and Flaviviruses in Association with Reduced MLKL Phosphorylation
papers.abstract: Emerging influenza viruses and mosquito-borne flaviviruses continue to challenge animal and public health, highlighting the need for antivirals that remain effective after infection. This study evaluated the in vitro activity of a 70% ethanolic whole-specimen extract of the marine bivalve Entodesma navicula (ENE) against influenza A/Puerto Rico/8/1934 (H1N1; A/PR8), A/Wisconsin/15/2009 (H3N2), influenza B/Florida/78/2015, Zika virus, and dengue virus serotype 2. Antiviral activity was assessed using time-of-addition analysis, viability-based cytopathic-effect assays, reverse-transcription quantitative PCR, infectious virus titration, immunofluorescence, Western blotting, and flow cytometry. In the A/PR8 model, pre- and co-treatment produced no consistent inhibition. By contrast, post-infection ENE suppressed all tested viruses. For A/PR8, Zika virus, and dengue virus, this activity was supported by reduced viral genome abundance, infectious progeny, and viral antigen expression. In A/PR8-infected A549 cells, ENE reduced phosphorylation of receptor-interacting serine/threonine-protein kinase 3 (RIPK3) and mixed lineage kinase domain-like pseudokinase (MLKL). ENE also reduced the proportion of cells positive for phosphorylated MLKL within Zika- and dengue-virus-infected Vero E6 populations. These findings identify E. navicula as an underexplored source of post-infection antiviral bioactivity associated with attenuated necroptosis-related signaling. Isolation of active constituents and causal validation in primary cells and animal models are needed.

papers.title: Comparative Veterinary Psychopharmacology in Dogs and Cats: Neurotransmitter Targets, Translational Boundaries, and Species-Specific Pharmacokinetics
papers.abstract: Behavioral disorders in companion animals are increasingly being managed with pharmacotherapy. However, prescription practices often rely on extrapolation from human psychiatry without considering species-specific phenotypes, diagnostic frameworks, or pharmacokinetic variability. A structured translational approach is required to align mechanistic plausibility with clinical evidence and interspecies constraints. This review consolidates the current information on the pharmacological modulation of neurotransmitter systems in canine and feline behavioral disorders using a comparative framework. Neurotransmitter circuits are mapped to relevant phenotypes. Controlled clinical evidence supports the use of selected serotonergic agents for specific chronic behavioral indications in dogs, whereas evidence in cats remains scarce and indication-specific. Controlled veterinary evidence is also available for selected agents used in acute or situational behavioral indications and for selegiline in canine cognitive dysfunction. Contrastingly, the broader neurotransmitter–phenotype relationships and emerging pharmacological targets discussed in this review are supported by mechanistic or translational evidence and should not be interpreted as established clinical indications. Cross-species translation is most defensible at the level of conserved receptors and transporters, whereas direct transfer of human diagnostic categories and subjective symptoms is limited in veterinary patients. Species- and drug-specific pharmacokinetic differences, along with limited feline data, necessitate careful dose initiation, titration, and monitoring to mitigate adverse effects and drug interactions. This review provides a structured framework for interpreting psychopharmacological evidence in dogs and cats by integrating pharmacological mechanisms, the design and scope of available clinical studies, translational boundaries, and species- and drug-specific pharmacokinetic considerations. Future research could benefit from standardized outcome measures, expanded feline trials, and pragmatic real-world designs.

papers.title: Development and Application of an eDNA-Based MIRA-LFD Assay for the Detection of the Chinhai Spiny Newt
papers.abstract: The Chinhai spiny newt (Echinotriton chinhaiensis) is a rare amphibian species endemic to China. Its specialized habitat and small size make conventional field surveys and population monitoring not only time-consuming and labor-intensive, but also challenging. To address this challenge, we developed a visual detection method for habitat monitoring by integrating environmental DNA (eDNA) analysis with multi-enzyme isothermal rapid amplification (MIRA) and lateral flow dipstick (LFD) technologies. A specific mitochondrial gene fragment was selected as a target. MIRA primers and probes were designed and optimized through comparative sequence analysis with sympatric species, including crucian carp, bullfrogs, and polar fire shrimp. The assay conditions were subsequently refined by optimizing reaction temperature and test strip development time. Results indicate that using aquatic eDNA as a template, the optimized MIRA system incubated at 37 °C for 30 min, followed by a 20 min LFD development, produces clear and interpretable results. The assay demonstrated a DNA detection limit of 5.1 × 10−4 ng/μL, corresponding to a sensitivity higher than that of conventional PCR. The complete MIRA-LFD procedure can be performed within 50 min, and its identification results are consistent with those from high-throughput sequencing. This established method enables specific, efficient, and rapid detection of the Chinhai spiny newt in aquatic environments. It provides a practical technical tool for habitat surveys of this species, improving efficiency while reducing labor and resource demands. Furthermore, this approach offers a potential reference for habitat studies of other rare animal species.

papers.title: Juvenile Spontaneous Mediastinal Hemorrhage with Suspect Trauma
papers.abstract: A 6-month-old intact female American Pitbull (Canis lupus familiaris) underwent forensic evaluation for suspected blunt force trauma. Postmortem computed tomography (PMCT) identified pleural hyperattenuating soft tissue attenuating material, consistent with clotted blood, pleural effusion, a large thymus, and moderate to severe cranial mediastinal expansion with mixed fluid and lower-attenuation, soft tissue attenuating material. Histology confirmed thymic hemorrhage, while autopsy identified hemothorax, pleural blood clots, and hemomediastinum, excluding trauma, most consistent with spontaneous idiopathic thymic hemorrhage. This case highlights the utility of identifying hyperattenuating clot formation on PMCT, like the sentinel clot sign, for localizing antemortem hemorrhage and improving antemortem-postmortem correlation in forensic investigations.

papers.title: Mango Peel Fermented with Ethanol-Industry Yeast Waste and Urea Modulates In Vitro Rumen Fermentation, Nutrient Degradability, and Methane Concentration
papers.abstract: This study evaluated mango peel co-fermented with fresh yeast waste from the ethanol industry and urea (YUFMP) as a ruminant supplement using the in vitro gas-production technique. A 2 × 4 factorial arrangement in a completely randomised design was used, with two roughage-to-concentrate (R:C) ratios (40:60 and 60:40; rice straw as roughage) and four YUFMP levels (0, 2%, 4%, and 6% of substrate dry matter, DM). Co-fermentation raised the crude protein of mango peel from 4.39% to 17.00% DM and reduced its total phenolic content from 100.30 to 73.49 mg GAE/g extract. The 40:60 ratio gave higher in vitro degradability of DM, organic matter, neutral detergent fibre (IVNDFD), and true DM (IVTD) than the 60:40 ratio at 12 and 24 h (p < 0.01), and higher total volatile fatty acids (VFA) at 24 h (65.56 vs. 57.16 mmol/L; p < 0.01). YUFMP increased asymptotic gas production from 87.85 to 100.47–102.58 mL/0.5 g DM (p < 0.01) and cumulative gas production at 12–96 h (p < 0.05), with linear and quadratic trends. At 24 h, IVNDFD and IVTD were highest at 6% YUFMP (47.90 and 69.30%; p < 0.05). The protozoal population declined linearly with YUFMP (12.75 to 9.00 × 105 cells/mL at 24 h; p < 0.01), as did CH4 concentration at 12 h (18.99 to 13.08%) and 24 h (23.21 to 14.93%; both p < 0.01), whereas absolute CH4 volume was unaffected (p > 0.05). YUFMP did not alter total VFA or VFA molar proportions at 24 h and reduced propionate linearly only at 12 h (p < 0.01), indicating that the lower CH4 concentration reflected dilution of CH4 within a larger volume of fermentation gas rather than a redirection of metabolic hydrogen towards propionate. Ruminal pH (6.87–7.04) and ammonia nitrogen were unaffected (p > 0.05). Inclusion at 2–4% DM is recommended for further in vivo evaluation.

papers.title: Daily and Seasonal Activity Patterns of the Endemic Balkan Snow Vole (Dinaromys bogdanovi) Within a Sympatric Small Mammal Community
papers.abstract: Understanding the temporal ecology of endemic species is important for conservation planning in biodiversity hotspots during global climate change and habitat alteration. We used three years of camera-trap monitoring across two deployment periods to quantify daily and seasonal activity patterns of the endemic Balkan snow vole (Dinaromys bogdanovi) and sympatric terrestrial small mammals in Biokovo Nature Park, Croatia, within the Western Balkan glacial refugia. Dinaromys bogdanovi was predominantly nocturnal, with minor but consistent diurnal activity, and shifted from multimodal nocturnal activity in spring, summer and autumn to a unimodal winter peak. Temporal niche differentiation occurred between D. bogdanovi and the sympatric small mammals during some seasons. These differences were associated with nocturnal peak timing and the greater diurnal activity of D. bogdanovi. In summer, the detected taxa showed greater overlap in predominantly nocturnal activity, consistent with a possible influence of thermal conditions on surface activity, although temperature was not measured. We also provide quantitative activity data for the geographically isolated Dinaric population of Eliomys quercinus. This study demonstrates the value of long-term camera trapping for monitoring cryptic small mammals and provides a baseline for evaluating future changes in activity, habitat use and community interactions, supporting conservation planning for endemic species facing climate change and anthropogenic pressures.
